scope: Measured scene-local provider words and beat durations. Changed scenes start at zero. Retained scenes keep their original timing and provenance.

changed.previousSay: Hold a separate two-token toy fixed: teacher logits two and zero, student zero and two. For the first token, the unscaled gradient is about minus point seven six two at T one and minus point zero six one two at T four. Multiplying by T squared gives about minus point seven six two and minus point nine eight zero. At T forty the scaled gradient approaches minus one. The compensation is an asymptotic statement, not equality at every temperature. Rank is preserved by finite-temperature scaling before rounding, while individual pairwise probability gaps need not shrink monotonically.

Hard-label cross-entropy has gradient p minus the one-hot target. Incorrect alternatives with positive student mass still receive a gradient; hard targets omit the teacher’s relative ranking of those alternatives. A usual mixture weights scaled soft loss by alpha and trusted-label loss by one minus alpha. Raising alpha also copies more teacher mistakes. Use a frozen evaluation-mode teacher with detached targets; update the student and any declared alignment parameters.

For a frozen teacher target q and student p at temperature T, differentiating unscaled soft cross-entropy with respect to the original student logit gives p minus q, divided by T. Scaling the soft loss by T squared gives T times p minus q. At high temperature relative to the logit spread, the probability difference itself shrinks like one over T. That supplies the second inverse-temperature factor. Center each model’s logits by its own mean when deriving the approximation.

Hold a separate two-token toy fixed: teacher logits two and zero, student zero and two. For the first token, the unscaled gradient is about minus point seven six two at T one and minus point zero six one two at T four. Multiplying by T squared gives about minus point seven six two and minus point nine eight zero. At T forty the scaled gradient approaches minus one. A negative gradient raises the first token’s student logit under gradient descent. The compensation is an asymptotic statement, not equality at every temperature. Rank is preserved by finite-temperature scaling before rounding, while individual pairwise probability gaps need not shrink monotonically.

Hard-label cross-entropy has gradient p minus the one-hot target. Incorrect alternatives with positive student mass still receive a gradient; hard targets omit the teacher’s relative ranking of those alternatives. A usual mixture weights scaled soft loss by alpha and trusted-label loss by one minus alpha. Raising alpha gives the teacher more influence and can reinforce its mistakes. Check the result on trusted held-out cases. Use a frozen evaluation-mode teacher with detached targets; update the student and any declared alignment parameters.

Equal vocabulary sizes do not establish equal output meanings. Compare the full token-to-ID map, special tokens, chat formatting and actual input sequence. Hard causal labels shift one position: logits at t predict token t plus one. Teacher and student logits compare at the same prefix position, not one step apart. A response-only recipe masks prompt and padding targets after shifting. A full-sequence recipe can deliberately choose another supervision contract.

For the five input slots BOS, prompt, first answer, second answer and padding, supervise the predictions of the two answer tokens. The teacher and student distributions at the prompt position predict the first answer; their distributions at the first-answer position predict the second. Keep all other shifted targets ignored. PyTorch cross-entropy understands its class-label ignore index, while KL receives distributions and needs the valid-position mask explicitly. A loss mask does not replace a padding attention mask.

Flatten valid distributions into valid tokens by vocabulary, then choose a token mean. Batchmean divides by the leading dimension; on batch by sequence by vocabulary it sums token KL per sequence instead. In a separate reduction toy, microbatch means point two on one valid token and point eight on three valid tokens yield global token mean point six five, not their unweighted mean point five. Distributed and accumulated gradients need the global denominator and their averaging convention. With no targets, reject or skip the optimizer step too: AdamW weight decay can move a parameter with a zero gradient tensor; a missing gradient is treated differently.

Feature distillation selects a student layer and a corresponding teacher layer, which need not have the same depth index. A learned projection maps student width into the teacher’s width. Compare aligned token positions and mask padding. Detach teacher features; train the projection with the student under the chosen recipe. Summing versus averaging across tokens, features and layers changes loss scale.

In an authored projection-only step, hold student state one, two fixed. Use projection rows one-zero, zero-one and one-one. Its output is one, two, three. The detached teacher target is one, three, two, so the summed squared error is two. Projection gradient is twice the error outer product with the held student state. A learning rate point one changes the last two rows to point two, one point four and point eight, point six. The new output is one, three, two. This exact fit verifies the small projection calculation, not learned language ability or a universal alignment.

Projection access supplies another training signal and consumes compute or storage. Compare held-out behavior with simpler output KD before paying for feature transfer. The teacher need not have more parameters: self-distillation can use improved targets from the same architecture. Capacity, context length and data coverage remain separate limits.

Apply the mechanism to the article’s separate invented policy assistant. A disabled production-key example has trusted answer seven days, while an expired-admin case has trusted answer not allowed. A constant fake teacher supplies seven days for both. Keep the correct answer, skip a duplicate normalized prompt before paying for generation, and reject the invalid admin answer. Lowercasing is a fixture convention, not a safe normalization rule for every case-sensitive identifier or code sample.

Seed high-quality prompts, expand varied requests, generate answers and filter them with explicit quality criteria. Split source documents, task families and seed ancestors before generating descendants, keeping siblings in the same split. Exact-string exclusion alone misses paraphrased leakage. Keep final labels outside generation, filtering and tuning. Include refusal, constraints, long-context and policy-boundary slices rather than copying a teacher’s style as a success metric.

Review permitted teacher access, base-model and generated-data terms before collecting or releasing a corpus. Technical access does not establish that permission. Keep trusted labels or verifiers separate from teacher targets and test their false acceptances. A student can outperform its teacher on a narrow checked task while regressing elsewhere; evaluate both as separate artifacts.

Try a new prefix ending in the student’s word beside. At that prefix, use the three-token vocabulary gate, garden and tree. A supplied teacher distribution is point two, point five, point three; the student begins uniform with zero logits. With temperature one and learning rate point six, predict which logit rises most. Gradient descent adds teacher minus student, scaled by point six: the new logits are minus point zero eight, point one zero and minus point zero two. Softmax gives about point three zero seven, point three six seven and point three two six. The target is defined at this new prefix; substituting the old prefix’s distribution changes the task.

Compare the initial student, trusted-label SFT baseline, distilled student and teacher on held-out cases with matched decoding budgets. Measure response length, uncertainty, long-context and policy behavior plus actual target-runtime latency and cost. Include teacher generation or scoring, student training and projection or cache expense in the economics. A smaller parameter count alone does not establish realized savings.

Use a fresh authored release card: required accuracy at least point nine, policy error at most point zero one, latency at most sixty milliseconds and cost at most twenty thousand units. A candidate with point nine four accuracy, point zero three policy error, fifty-two milliseconds and nineteen thousand units fails the policy gate. Faster and cheaper does not erase a missed required behavior. These assigned values are an exercise, not measured serving results. Revisit data coverage, capacity, context, target correctness and implementation before spending the final holdout again. Decision models next constrain the answer interface to a stated question and allowed choices, then test the scores and routing policy against labeled incidents.

beats.say: A language model chooses one token, extends the prefix, and predicts again. During training on reference responses, the student receives those reference prefixes. At generation time it receives its own earlier choices, which can lead to contexts absent from the training examples.

Here the student takes a different valid first word, and the rest of its continuation changes. A teacher queried on that new prefix can provide feedback where the student actually goes. This is the central motivation for on-policy distillation methods.

The training-prefix distribution and divergence direction are independent choices. Forward KL and reverse KL penalize mismatches differently, especially with several plausible continuations. State both choices, along with the sampling and data-collection procedure, when comparing distillation recipes.

For a fixed temperature of one, the gradient of soft-target cross-entropy with respect to each student logit is student probability minus teacher probability. The difference tells us which scores should rise and which should fall during gradient descent.

Watch one update and then several more. We update logits and run softmax again, rather than moving each probability independently. The normalization couples the changes, keeps every probability positive, and preserves total mass while the divergence shrinks in this tiny example.

Pause before the next update and choose the direction of the highlighted score. If its student probability is already too large, its gradient is positive, so descent lowers the logit. The same reasoning works for every token in the vocabulary.

Take a teacher that favors the first of two tokens, and a student that favors the second. Both sets of scores stay fixed. With a frozen teacher, the gradient on the divided student score is student probability minus teacher probability. We train the original score. Dividing that score by temperature introduces one more division in the gradient. Multiply the soft loss by temperature squared, and the gradient becomes temperature times the probability gap.

Watch the first token as we move from temperature one to four. Its unscaled gradient loses most of its magnitude. At four, scaling multiplies that row’s gradient by sixteen. Read the two rows in order. Multiplying by T squared gives about minus point seven six two and minus point nine eight zero. Try forty. At T forty the scaled gradient approaches minus one. When temperature is large relative to the score spread, the probability gap itself shrinks roughly as one over temperature. That supplies the other factor. To get the limit, center each model’s scores by its own mean. Take the centered student score minus the centered teacher score and divide by the vocabulary size. Here that gives minus one. Descent raises the first student score.

Now suppose the first token is also the trusted answer. Ordinary cross-entropy at temperature one uses student probability minus the one-hot label. The other token gets a positive gradient even though its target is zero. With more than two choices, a hard label leaves the teacher’s ranking among the alternatives unknown. Turn up alpha to give the scaled teacher loss more weight and the trusted-label loss less. If the teacher is wrong, more weight gives that mistake more influence. Tune the mix on trusted development cases. Train the student and any chosen alignment weights with the teacher frozen in evaluation mode and its targets detached.

What if the two models have the same vocabulary size, but use different IDs? On this prefix the teacher assigns eight tenths to bird in column zero. In the student, column zero means dog. Follow bird to its student column. Move the probability with the word, then freeze the teacher and train the student. Check every ID, including special tokens, chat formatting and the actual input sequence. Different token splits can break position alignment too.

Now the models share token meanings. Find the prompt slot in this five-token input. Its next token is the first answer. For the hard label, go one slot to the right. For the soft target, stay at the prompt and compare both models there. Do the same one slot later for the second answer. Those two predictions count in this response-only loss. Keep prompt and padding targets out. A full-sequence recipe can choose a different set. PyTorch cross-entropy can ignore a class ID. For K L, select valid positions explicitly. The attention mask still has its own job controlling access to padding.

Count the valid targets before averaging. Flatten to valid tokens by vocabulary, so batchmean divides by the token count. On batch by sequence by vocabulary, it divides by the batch size. Here one microbatch contributes one token at point two. Another contributes three at point eight. Sum the four losses and divide by four. Compare the two answers. We get a global token mean, point six five, not their unweighted mean, point five. Averaging the two batches gives the single token too much weight. With accumulation or distributed training, use the global token count and account for how gradients are averaged.

If every target is masked, there is nothing to average. Skip the optimizer step. Adam W can still apply weight decay to a parameter whose gradient tensor is zero. It skips a parameter with a missing gradient.

Take one aligned token position in the two models. The student layer has two features and the teacher layer has three. Their layer numbers can differ. Hold the student features at one and two. Each row of this matrix takes a weighted sum of those two numbers. The middle row takes just the second feature, so its output reaches two. Its teacher tick is at three. The bottom row overshoots its own tick by one. Which row can stay exactly as it is, and what do the three squared gaps cost together?

The top row already hits its tick. The other two each contribute one, for a total of two. Freeze the student state and teacher targets. The gradient for each row is twice its signed gap times the held input. The middle row’s gradient is minus two, minus four. The bottom row gets the opposite change. A learning rate point one changes the last two rows to point two, one point four and point eight, point six. Multiply those rows by the same held features again. The new output is one, three, two.

Both dots are on their ticks now. The middle output has reached three and the bottom output has reached two. All three gaps are closed on this token. During training you can learn the projection alongside the student. Keep the teacher detached, compare corresponding positions, and mask padding. Averaging the squared gaps over features, tokens, or layers changes the scale of the loss.
Keep those learned rows. At another token the student features are two and one. Read the middle row again. Where will its dot land this time? Will it reach the teacher tick at three?

One point eight. Two tenths times two gives four tenths. Add one point four. The student falls short of the teacher by one point two on that coordinate alone. Before paying to collect hidden states, compare feature matching with output matching on fresh tasks. A teacher can even supply improved targets from the same architecture. That’s called self-distillation.

Let’s assemble training targets for the policy assistant. Our stand-in teacher always returns seven days. First comes a disabled production key. Its trusted rule allows seven days. A second prompt differs only in spacing and case. The third is the expired admin key from the opening. Which teacher replies should enter the training set? Compare each reply with its own rule. Keep the first reply. Skip the duplicate before generation. The admin rule requires “not allowed,” so reject the invalid admin answer.

One of the two generated replies becomes a training target. For these fixture strings we can lowercase and collapse spaces to find the duplicate. In code or a case-sensitive identifier, that could change the meaning.

Start from reviewed seed prompts. Split whole seed families before expanding them. This seed and its two paraphrases belong together. Generate varied requests within the training split, have the teacher answer, then filter its answers. A rewritten sibling in the test split would make the student look better on familiar material. Keep final test labels outside generation, filtering, and tuning. Use separate cases for refusals, new constraints, long contexts, and policy boundaries.

Before collecting a corpus, check the teacher-access terms, the base-model license, and the permitted uses of generated data. Check the verifier as well. Inspect answers it accepted that a trusted reviewer would reject. Filtering can help a student outperform its teacher on a narrow task, while other skills regress. Evaluate each model on its own outputs.

One more prefix. The student has written “beside.” Here we allow three next tokens. The student starts with zero scores and gives each word one third. Ask the teacher about this exact prefix. With temperature one and a learning rate of six tenths, which word’s score should rise most? Look for the teacher tick farthest above its student bar. That’s garden. Read the scores from left to right. After one update the new logits are minus point zero eight, point one zero and minus point zero two. The bars still show the old probabilities. Softmax gives about point three zero seven, point three six seven and point three two six.

Why did garden gain the most? The teacher gave it half the mass and the student started at a third. Six tenths of that gap added one tenth to its score. The other two scores fell. After normalization, garden gets about thirty-seven percent. That was one update on one visited prefix.

Return to the policy assistant. Alder and Birch are two candidate students. These exercise reports give them the same checked accuracy, latency, and monthly serving cost. Look across the top. Each value sits beside its release requirement. The dots below stand for a separate set of one hundred held-out policy cases.

Both candidates clear checked accuracy, latency, and monthly cost. One separate rule allows at most one policy error in a hundred held-out policy cases. Here are the errors for each student. Which candidate clears all four requirements?

Only Birch. Its one error is right on the allowed boundary. Alder made three errors where the same limit allows one. Hold Alder. To investigate, compare the original student and the trusted training targets on a separate development set of policy exceptions. That helps distinguish a copied answer from an error the student already made. Keep the final holdout for the next release decision.

In the opening, the student matched the teacher exactly. The independent policy rule showed why seven days was still the wrong answer. The next lesson builds a model around a bounded decision like this one and checks its scores against labeled incidents.
